PA3605 Cosmology: additional material for Lecture 5

The scale factor and the Hubble “constant”

The Friedmann equation provides a physical explanation for the (empirical) Hubble law. The recession velocity of a point in the Universe 𝐯=d⁢𝐫/d⁢t, and isotropy requires that 𝐯 be in the same direction as 𝐫. If we use non-bold symbols to denote the magnitudes of vectors (i.e., r=|𝐫|), we can therefore write

𝐯=r˙⁢𝐫^ (1)

where 𝐫^ is the unit vector in the 𝐫-direction (𝐫^=𝐫/r). We can can write Equation 1 as

𝐯=r˙r⁢𝐫 (2)

Recalling that 𝐫=a⁢(t)⁢𝐱 and 𝐫˙=a˙⁢(t)⁢𝐱, we find

𝐯=a˙a⁢𝐫 (3)

which is the Hubble law 𝐯=H⁢𝐫, with

H⁢(t)=a˙a (4)

This explicitly associates the (observed) Hubble law with the expansion of the Universe. It also allows us to re-cast the Friedmann equation in terms of H⁢(t)

H2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ−k⁢c2a2 (5)

Note that H is not a constant: in realistic cosmologies, H decreases as the Universe expands. By convention we call H⁢(t) the Hubble parameter, and use the symbol H0 (the “Hubble constant”) to denote the present-day value of H.

Expansion and redshift

To relate the expansion of the Universe to the (observable) redshift, we consider two points (or galaxies) separated by a small distance d⁢r. Hubble’s law tells us that their relative velocity d⁢v=H⁢d⁢r=(a˙/a)⁢d⁢r. This velocity leads to photons being Doppler shifted (to longer wavelengths, as d⁢v is positive), and as d⁢r is small we can use the linear approximation for the Doppler shift. The change in wavelength is therefore

d⁢λλe=d⁢vc (6)

where λe is the emitted photon wavelength. The travel time between the emitting galaxy and the observer d⁢t=d⁢r/c, and we substitute to find

d⁢λλe=H⁢d⁢rc=a˙a⁢d⁢rc=a˙a⁢d⁢t (7)

Recalling that a˙=d⁢a/d⁢t, we see that

d⁢λλe=d⁢aa (8)

and therefore λ∝a. The observed wavelength of a photon therefore increases linearly with the scale-factor a. We defined the redshift z by

z=Δ⁢λλe=λo−λeλe (9)

which we can re-arrange as

1+z=λoλe=a⁢(to)a⁢(te) (10)

By convention we define z=0 and a=1 to be the present-day Universe, so the (dimensionless) scale-factor is related to the redshift by

a⁢(t)=11+z (11)

We therefore see that if we observe a galaxy with redshift z=1, we are looking back to a time when the Universe was half its current size (i.e., a⁢(t)=1/2).

This simplified derivation is strictly only valid in the limit of small distances, but a rigorous relativistic treatment actually yields exactly the same result in the general case. The complete derivation (starting from the metric) can be found in Section A2.1 of Liddle, or Section 3.6 of Ryden.
